function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a CI script).  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repository.  
Because I can’t actually clone or push the repo from here, you’ll have to run the commands locally.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you don’t have SSH keys set up, use the HTTPS URL instead:
> `git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Node.js app (most likely listening on port 3000).  
A minimal, production‑ready Dockerfile looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and contains the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a clean install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The container only contains the production dependencies, keeping the image lean.

> **If the app uses a different start script** (e.g. `node server.js`), change the `CMD` line accordingly.

---

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Below is a combined Deployment + Service manifest that matches the repo’s typical Node.js port (3000).  
Feel free to adjust the `replicas`, `image`, or `serviceType` as needed.

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **Where to put it?**  
> Create a folder called `k8s/` (or `deploy/`) at the repo root and drop the file there.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions – Build & Push

Create a workflow that builds the Docker image and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) whenever you push to `main`.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache

    - name: Image digest
      run: echo "Image pushed with digest ${{ steps.docker_build.outputs.digest }}"
```

> **What this does**  
> * Checks out the repo.  
> * Logs into GHCR using the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN`.  
> * Builds the image with caching for faster subsequent builds.  
> * Pushes the image to `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`.  
> * You can later reference this image in the Kubernetes manifest.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
# From the repo root
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you want to keep the Kubernetes files in a separate folder, make sure the folder exists first:
> `mkdir -p k8s` (or `deploy`).

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to GHCR.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Build locally** (optional but recommended):

   ```bash
   docker build -t nodejs-welcome:local .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 nodejs-welcome:local
   ```

   Visit `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is reachable.

2. **Deploy to a cluster** (if you have `kubectl` configured):

   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

   Verify pods are running:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome
   ```

   And expose the service (if you want external access):

   ```bash
   kubectl expose deployment nodejs-welcome --type=LoadBalancer --name=nodejs-welcome-lb
   ```

---

That’s it! 🎉  
You now have a Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a CI pipeline that automatically builds and publishes your Node.js app whenever you push to `main`. If you run into any hiccups, feel free to ask.
